A1.justification: Both PDFs describe WEBDEVJUDGE and retain identifiable corresponding methods, experiments, and analyses. All 27 pages of v1 and 33 pages of v2, including appendices, support comparison through readable text, tables, equations, and figures.

before.justification: v1 reports original annotation-agreement measurements, evaluator experiments on WEBDEVJUDGE, and feasibility-verification results on WEBDEVJUDGE-Unit.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark experiments and reports additional ensemble comparisons, prediction-consistency measurements, and evaluator case studies.

M1.justification: v1 suggests combining code-based reasoning with interactive verification. v2 implements this suggestion as an ensemble: LLM judgments handle intention and static criteria, while dynamic judgments combine agent and LLM outputs using Boolean OR (Section 4.3, Equation 2). The original evaluator pipeline remains.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the 654-instance WEBDEVJUDGE across the same three domains and the 502-task WEBDEVJUDGE-Unit. Added ensembles and case studies stay within this coverage. Revised preference-label counts do not establish new task or domain coverage.

E2.justification: The evaluator rosters in the main benchmark, modality comparisons, and WEBDEVJUDGE-Unit remain unchanged. New Table 7 adds GPT-4.1 and DeepSeek-V3-0324 ensembles with UI-TARS-1.5, explicitly comparing them against their standalone LLM counterparts.

E3.justification: v1 Appendix B.2 versus v2 Appendix C.2 changes the Likert preference threshold from 2 to 1 and intention/static/dynamic rubric weights from 1:1:1 to 1:3:2. The reported interaction-filter exclusion changes from scores above 8 to scores below 8. These materially revise documented filtering and judgment procedures; they do not establish whether model inference was rerun.

E4.justification: v2 substantially extends diagnostics through the ensemble comparison testing complementary evaluator strengths (Table 7), rubric-based inter-model and rubric-versus-direct consistency analyses (Figures 7–8), and rubric-quality and evaluator-failure case studies (Figures 9–11). The earlier positional-bias, modality, and non-tie analyses are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests for these experiments. Updated agreement percentages and additional prediction-consistency matrices change results, not uncertainty-reporting practices.

E6.justification: Results change throughout Tables 1 and 3–5, Figure 3, and the debiasing and non-tie appendices. Table 3 changes from GPT-4.1 and Claude-4-Sonnet jointly scoring 66.06% to 70.34% and 70.18%, respectively. Preference counts change from 258/258/138 to 269/276/109. Ensemble and consistency results are added; Table 6 remains unchanged. Revised settings and labels preclude interpreting these as same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: v2 adds the mathematical definition of dynamic ensemble fusion, Res_dynamic = Agent OR LLM (Equation 2). This is a limited formal addition; no new theorem, proof, or theoretical guarantee accompanies it.

C1.justification: The benchmark contribution and human–model reliability gap remain central. v2 narrows the 89.7% annotation-agreement statement to a sampled subset, uses 'over 80%' in the introduction, and changes the claimed human–model discrepancy from exceeding 15% to about 15%.

C2.justification: New Appendix A acknowledges subjectivity, possible demographic or professional biases from the small annotation pool, and limited benchmark scale. Section 4.3 also interprets the new ensemble results as evidence that static reasoning and interactive verification can complement each other. Earlier failure-mechanism explanations largely remain.

D1.justification: v2 discloses intermediate filtering counts and the 700-instance annotation sample (Table 8), full rubric and Likert comparison prompts (Appendix C.4), and a concrete rubric-generation example. These extend existing documentation. Conversely, explicit reasoning-model temperatures are replaced by the unspecified statement that temperatures were set 'accordingly'.

R1.justification: Li et al.'s 'Patterns over Principles' citation and reference are removed. The substantive positioning relative to existing judge benchmarks and agent-based evaluation work remains largely unchanged.

P1.justification: The main narrative is largely retained with localized wording and caption edits. Appendices are reorganized, including reversing the order of positional-bias and prediction-consistency discussions and adding dedicated limitations, prompt-template, and case-study sections. Author order, publication headers, and acknowledgments also change.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the visual presentation with ensemble and filtering tables (Tables 7–8), paired consistency heatmaps (Figures 7–8), rubric examples (Figure 9), and detailed screenshot-and-response failure panels (Figures 10–11). Existing displays are largely retained, with revised captions, prompt-box formatting, and appendix placement.

improvement.justification: The filtering documentation, full judgment prompts, concrete failure examples, and explicit annotation limitations make v2 easier to inspect and interpret. The additional ensemble and consistency analyses provide useful supporting evidence. These are limited net gains: exact reasoning-model temperatures are lost, and the preference-label revisions are not explained. Higher scores under revised settings do not themselves establish better paper quality.
